summary: Specifies how DNS can store E.164 telephone numbers and find services tied to a number. It brings ENUM in line with the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System, and obsoletes RFC 2916. It must be read alongside the documents described in RFC 3401. It was replaced by RFC 6116 and RFC 6117.

plainLanguage.summary: ENUM lets a phone number be looked up in the DNS. The number is rewritten into a name under e164.arpa, and the records stored there say which kinds of service that number reaches and give the address to use. The result is normally a URI such as a SIP address, which the calling program then resolves in the ordinary way.

questions: how to look up phone numbers in dns
how does an enum naptr record work
subtitle: Using the DNS to answer what services are reachable at a telephone number.

tldr.problem: There was no standard way to look up what a telephone number could be used for, such as whether it reached a voice-over-IP address, a messaging service or a fax.
tldr.mechanism: ENUM turns an E.164 number into a DNS name by stripping the digits, separating them with dots and reversing them under e164.arpa. The DNS is then asked for NAPTR records at that name, and their rewrite rules produce a URI such as a SIP address.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3761 is a Proposed Standard from April 2004 and has been obsoleted by RFC 6116 and RFC 6117, which cover the E.164 to URI mapping.

facts.label: Service field prefix
facts.value: E2U+, followed by one or more Enumservices

today: RFC 3761 is a Proposed Standard from April 2004, and it has been obsoleted by RFC 6116 and RFC 6117, which cover the E.164 to URI mapping. The RFC itself notes that it obsoletes RFC 2916 to bring ENUM in line with the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System described in RFC 3401, and that it cannot be read or understood without the documents RFC 3401 discusses.

sections.title: Storing Phone Numbers in the DNS
sections.content:
ENUM uses the DNS to answer the question of what can be done with a telephone number. A number written in the international format defined by ITU-T Recommendation E.164 is turned into a DNS name, and the DNS is asked for NAPTR records at that name. Those records hold rewrite rules that turn the number into a URI, such as a SIP address, and the protocol behind that URI is then resolved to find the host to contact.

Because the e164.arpa domain is divided into subdomains, the work of holding the records is spread out. A holder of a number contacts the zone administrator for its part of the namespace, and the SOA record of the zone says who that is, in the same way as any other DNS zone. Policies for what may be listed differ from one part of the world to another.

The RFC is a rewrite of RFC 2916, made to fit the Dynamic Delegation Discovery System that RFC 3401 describes, and it says outright that it cannot be read without the documents RFC 3401 lists. The RFC also allows the same mechanisms to be used for private dialing plans, with two conditions: the suffix must not be e164.arpa, and the use must not be called ENUM.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is to reuse the DNS rather than invent a new directory for phone numbers. Each part of the e164.arpa zone is administered separately, following the numbering plan, so the records for a country's numbers are held by whoever administers that part of the namespace.

sections.title: Turning a Number into a Domain Name
sections.content:
The Application Unique String is the fully qualified E.164 number with every non-digit character removed, except the leading plus sign, which is kept as an anchor so the string is not confused with other kinds of telephone number. The number +44-116-496-0348 therefore becomes +441164960348.

The first well known rule of ENUM is the identity rule: its output equals its input. The RFC explains why this is possible: the E.164 namespace and the databases holding it are organized so that the name alone points at the finest level of the namespace, and no rewriting is needed to get there.

To turn that string into a DNS key, four steps are applied. Remove every character except the digits, so +442079460148 becomes 442079460148. Put a dot between each digit, giving 4.4.2.0.7.9.4.6.0.1.4.8. Reverse the order of the digits, giving 8.4.1.0.6.4.9.7.0.2.4.4. Finally append .e164.arpa, giving 8.4.1.0.6.4.9.7.0.2.4.4.e164.arpa. That name is what the client asks about, and the records it finds may hold the final result or, when the flags field is blank, new keys to look up in turn.
sections.plainLanguage: Converting a number to a name is a fixed four-step recipe: drop everything but the digits, put a dot between each digit, reverse the order, and add the suffix. One digit becomes one label of the DNS name, so the number and the name carry the same information in a shape the DNS can hold.

sections.title: The Service Field and Enumservices
sections.content:
The service field of a NAPTR record carries the E2U marker and one or more Enumservices. E2U is not optional: it is there so that ENUM rewrite rules cannot collide with rewrite rules of other kinds, and the RFC separately requires that the E2U part of the service field not be used for numbers that are not E.164 numbers. Each Enumservice begins with a plus sign and has the form type, optionally followed by colon-separated subtypes, where the type and each subtype are up to 32 letters or digits.

An Enumservice names a class of functionality and the URI schemes that may come back for it. There is no implicit link between the text of a type or subtype and any URI scheme or protocol: the mapping has to be written into the registration of that Enumservice. A registration of a type must also say which subtypes are allowed, and there is no concept of a registered subtype outside the type it belongs to. The one exception to the registration rule is for experimental names, which start with the facet X- and are to be used only with the active agreement of the parties involved.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record says what kind of service it is offering, with a label such as sip or h323. Those labels are only names: nothing links the word sip to the SIP protocol unless the registration for it says so, and the registration must also list which subtypes are allowed.

sections.title: How the Lookup Proceeds
sections.content:
A NAPTR record carries flags, and ENUM defines one: U. When the U flag is present the rule is the last one, and its output is a URI, which ends the DDDS loop. If the flag is absent the rule is non-terminal, and the client must use the key that the rule produced as the new key, querying the DNS again for more NAPTR records. A client that meets a flag it does not know must ignore the record and move to the next rule, and that test takes precedence over the ordering, because a new flag could change how the rest of the record is read.

The loop always ends in a single URI in absolute form. The RFC is explicit that the algorithm returns one rule; an application may show several results or pick faster, but that must not change how the algorithm runs.

Two NAPTR fields control which record a client uses. The Order field says in what order the records are to be interpreted, because DNS does not guarantee the order of the records in an answer. The RFC warns that a shorter matching rule placed before a longer one can mask it, which is why the order is a request from the holder of the number that the client must follow. The Preference field is only a suggestion that one record might be better than another, and the client may take it on advisement.
sections.plainLanguage: A lookup can take more than one step. Each record either finishes the job by handing back a URI, or it hands back another name to look up. Two numbers in the record decide which one a client picks: the order, which the client has to follow, and the preference, which it may ignore.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC's security section starts from the fact that DNS is not secure in its current form, so nothing in the answer can be shown to be authentic. As ENUM is deployed on the global Internet it is expected to be a popular target, and attacking the DNS is one way of attacking ENUM.

The threats it lists against DNS come from a threat analysis of the DNS: packet interception, including man-in-the-middle attacks and spoofed responses that beat the real one back to the resolver; ID guessing and query prediction, which the RFC notes is practical because the DNS header ID field is only 16 bits and the DNS server port is well known, leaving 2 to the power 32 combinations; name-based attacks that use caching behaviour to insert bad data; betrayal by a trusted server, which is often the one supplied by an ISP; and denial of service, against which DNS servers can also act as amplifiers because response packets are longer than query packets. A further risk is authenticated denial of domain names: a missing record can itself be used to change call routing policy.

Most of these can be addressed by authenticating the data with DNSSEC, but denial of service cannot, and a service that uses ENUM for address translation should still authenticate its peers rather than trusting the addressing mechanism. The RFC also warns about caching: a change can take as long to propagate as the time to live of the NAPTR records, which matters where addresses are for hire. Where several providers offer call routing in one numbering environment, the systems that accept changes need proper identification and authorization of whoever is making them.
sections.plainLanguage: ENUM inherits every weakness of the DNS, and the RFC lists the main ones: someone can intercept or forge the answer, or poison the cache. Signing the records with DNSSEC fixes most of that, but not denial of service, and a program using ENUM to find an address should still check who it is talking to.

sections.title: Registering an Enumservice
sections.content:
Every Enumservice has to be registered before it can be used. A registration names the type and its subtypes, the URI schemes that may be returned, a functional specification, security considerations, the intended usage and the author. The whole thing has to be published as an RFC on the Standards Track, an Experimental RFC or a BCP, and approved by the IESG. Once that happens IANA registers the Enumservice and points at the RFC.

The functional requirement is that a registered Enumservice can act as a selection mechanism when choosing one NAPTR record from another, so it must say what is expected when that record is used and what URI comes out of it. The security requirement is that every registration carries an analysis of its security issues, and that a statement of no known security issues must not be confused with a statement that the issues have not been assessed. The RFC lists three things such an analysis should look at: directives that can cause actions on a user's resources, which can even produce an endless loop in the resolution of a number; directives that disclose information; and Enumservices used by applications that need security assurance but supply none of their own.

On the DNS side, IANA was asked to delegate e164.arpa following instructions from the IAB, and names in the zone are to be delegated in line with Recommendation E.164. Delegations within the zone, as opposed to delegations of the zone itself, should follow expert review with a designated expert appointed by the IESG. Enumservice registrations are never deleted; one that is no longer appropriate is declared OBSOLETE by a new RFC that changes its intended use field.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody may invent a service label and start using it. The label has to be written up, published as an RFC and approved, and the write-up must say which URI schemes it may return and what the security risks are. The RFC also says how the zone itself is delegated and who reviews new delegations inside it.

data.title: NAPTR service field
data.code:
service-field = "E2U" 1*(servicespec)
servicespec   = "+" enumservice
enumservice   = type 0*(subtypespec)
subtypespec   = ":" subtype
type          = 1*32(ALPHA / DIGIT)
subtype       = 1*32(ALPHA / DIGIT)
